about.title: Arvin Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: Arvin residents rely on a small network of local clinics and often travel into the broader Kern County medical system for specialty or hospital care. When that care falls below the accepted standard — a missed diagnosis, a surgical mistake, a medication mix-up — the resulting harm can be permanent and hard to untangle on your own. California's MICRA rules make these cases procedurally demanding: a qualified medical expert almost always has to review the case, a 90-day pre-suit notice is generally required before filing, and the filing window is short. A bad medical outcome by itself doesn't mean malpractice occurred; the question is whether the provider deviated from the accepted standard of care. We can evaluate your medical records, determine whether the standard of care was met, and explain what steps and deadlines apply to your situation.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney Before the Clock Runs Out

items.title: Strict, Short Deadlines Under MICRA
items.desc: California generally gives you one year from when you discover the harm, and never more than three years from the injury itself, to bring a claim. We can help you figure out where you stand on that timeline before options close.

items.title: A 90-Day Notice Almost Always Comes First
items.desc: Before a malpractice lawsuit can even be filed in California, the provider typically must receive 90 days' written notice. Missing or mishandling this step can delay or jeopardize a claim, so early legal input matters.

items.title: Expert Review Is Required, Not Optional
items.desc: California law generally requires a qualified medical expert to support a malpractice claim. We can help arrange that review and assess whether the standard of care was actually violated.

items.question: I had a bad outcome after treatment in Arvin — does that mean malpractice happened?
items.answer: Not necessarily. California law requires proof that the provider's care fell below the accepted medical standard, not just that the result was disappointing or unexpected. We can review your records to help determine whether the standard of care was actually breached.

items.question: How long do I have to bring a medical malpractice claim in California?
items.answer: Generally, you have one year from when you discover the injury, and no more than three years from the date it occurred, whichever comes first. There's also typically a 90-day notice requirement before filing suit, so it's worth getting an evaluation sooner rather than later.

items.question: Do you handle my malpractice claim directly?
items.answer: We work on a contingency basis, meaning there's no fee unless you recover. We handle these cases and can evaluate whether you have a claim under California law.
